title: Country risk and emerging markets

sourceRefs.section: DCF — WACC and Cost of Equity
Discounted Cash Flow — Cost of Capital

objectives: Answer out loud: How would you adjust WACC for an emerging-market company?

steps.body: Investing in emerging markets carries extra risk: currency, political, sovereign default.
Add a country risk premium (CRP) to cost of equity.
Match the currency of the cash flows and the discount rate.

blocks.caption: CAPM with a country risk premium

blocks.template: A common CRP estimate uses the country's sovereign bond {{1}} over US Treasuries
USD cash flows should be discounted with a {{1}} discount rate

blocks.title: How do you estimate a country risk premium?
blocks.teaser: Simplest: the spread of the country's USD-denominated government bonds over US Treasuries.
blocks.body:
Simplest: the spread of the country's USD-denominated government bonds over US Treasuries. A refinement scales that spread by how much more volatile the country's stock market is than its bond market. Damodaran publishes country risk premiums annually.

**Interview answer:** "Start with the country's sovereign bond spread over Treasuries, sometimes scaled for equity market volatility, and add it to the cost of equity."

blocks.title: Where does the CRP go in CAPM?
blocks.teaser: Usually added to the cost of equity: Re = Rf + β × ERP + CRP.
blocks.body: Usually added to the cost of equity: Re = Rf + β × ERP + CRP. Some apply it via beta (exposure-weighted), reflecting that a company exporting most of its output is less exposed to local risk.

blocks.title: Should a company's country risk depend on where it's headquartered or where it sells?
blocks.body: Where it operates and earns. A Singapore-listed company with most revenue in Indonesia carries Indonesian risk.

blocks.title: Why does currency matching matter?
blocks.teaser: Local-currency cash flows include local inflation expectations; so must the discount rate.
blocks.body: Local-currency cash flows include local inflation expectations; so must the discount rate. Discount Indonesian rupiah cash flows at a rupiah-based rate (or convert cash flows to USD using forward rates and use a USD rate). Mixing them misstates value.

blocks.prompt: You're valuing an Indonesian company's rupiah cash flows. Which discount rate is consistent?

options.text: A USD WACC built on US Treasuries
A rupiah-based discount rate (or convert the cash flows to USD at forward rates)
Any rate, as long as you add a country risk premium
The US WACC minus expected inflation

blocks.explanation: Local-currency cash flows embed local inflation, so the discount rate must too — or convert the cash flows to USD and use a USD rate.

blocks.title: What if the local government bond market is thin or unreliable?
blocks.teaser: Build the local risk-free rate synthetically: the US Treasury yield plus the expected inflation differential between the two countries.
blocks.body: Build the local risk-free rate synthetically: the US Treasury yield plus the expected inflation differential between the two countries.
